    Bias detection in classification¶

    This walkthrough is adapted for teaching from our applications to fairness tutorial given at FAccT.

    The usecase is the BIOS dataset, where biographies of people are classified into occupations. Our goal will be to detect if there is any gender bias in the model classification. For that we will use interpreto.

    There are several parts to this notebook:

    1. Setting up the environment, loading the dataset and the model
    2. Attributions
    3. Probing the gender concept
    4. Unsupervised concepts analysis

    authors: Antonin Poché & Fanny Jourdan

    0. Setup¶

    0.1 Setting up the environment¶

    0.2 Loading the dataset¶

    We use the BIOS dataset from HuggingFace in streaming mode. We keep 1,000 training biographies and 1,000 test biographies for probing and concept analysis, and reuse the test subset for global attributions. We also read far enough into the test stream to include the three worked examples. These small subsets are loaded once, without downloading the full dataset.

    Paper: De-Artega et al. - FAccT 2019 - A Case Study of Semantic Representation Bias in a High-Stakes Setting

    In [4]:

train_genders = torch.tensor([sample["gender"] for sample in train_samples])

    1. Attributions¶

    Attribution highlight the most important inputs for a given prediction.

    1.1 Find representative examples¶

    We cannot check explanations for all examples, so we need to choose a few representative examples. In theory we should cover several elements of each class with both errors and correct predictions.

    In practice, let's focus on few errors. You are free to explore on your own.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    studied_ids = [107, 155]
studied_preds = [10, 13]

studied_samples = [test_samples[i] for i in studied_ids]
studied_texts = [sample["hard_text"] for sample in studied_samples]
studied_labels = [sample["profession"] for sample in studied_samples]
    studied_ids = [107, 155] studied_preds = [10, 13] studied_samples = [test_samples[i] for i in studied_ids] studied_texts = [sample["hard_text"] for sample in studied_samples] studied_labels = [sample["profession"] for sample in studied_samples]

    1.2 Compute attributions¶

    We use LIME, a perturbation-based attribution method, to explain both the true label and the predicted class for each studied example.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    from interpreto import Lime, plot_attributions

# Construct the explainer
explainer = Lime(model, tokenizer, n_perturbations=200)

# Explain both the label and prediction logits for each studied samples
attributions = {}
targets = torch.tensor([[label, pred] for label, pred in zip(studied_labels, studied_preds, strict=True)])
attributions["Lime"] = explainer.explain(studied_texts, targets)

for a in attributions["Lime"]:
    plot_attributions(a, classes_names=classes_names)
    from interpreto import Lime, plot_attributions # Construct the explainer explainer = Lime(model, tokenizer, n_perturbations=200) # Explain both the label and prediction logits for each studied samples attributions = {} targets = torch.tensor([[label, pred] for label, pred in zip(studied_labels, studied_preds, strict=True)]) attributions["Lime"] = explainer.explain(studied_texts, targets) for a in attributions["Lime"]: plot_attributions(a, classes_names=classes_names)

    1.3 Check with other methods¶

    No single attribution method is best in every setting. We compare LIME with Integrated Gradients (gradient-based) and Occlusion (perturbation-based) to see whether they highlight similar words.

    from interpreto import IntegratedGradients, Occlusion

for method in [IntegratedGradients, Occlusion]:

    explainer = method(model, tokenizer)
    attributions[method.__name__] = explainer.explain(studied_texts, targets)
    for a in attributions[method.__name__]:
        plot_attributions(a, classes_names=classes_names)

    1.4 Apply metrics¶

    Interpreto proposes the Deletion and Insertion metrics to evaluate the faithfulness of attributions. The idea is to remove or add tokens in their order of importance and check if it impacts the output coherently.

    Note that in practice, the more samples you have the more robust will the score be.

    Paper: Petsiuk et al. - ICLR 2018 - RISE: Randomized Input Sampling for Explanation of Black-box Models

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    from interpreto.attributions.metrics import Deletion

metric = Deletion(model, tokenizer)

for method_name, attribution in attributions.items():
    score,_ = metric.evaluate(attribution)
    print(f"{method_name} deletion score: {score:.4f}")
    from interpreto.attributions.metrics import Deletion metric = Deletion(model, tokenizer) for method_name, attribution in attributions.items(): score,_ = metric.evaluate(attribution) print(f"{method_name} deletion score: {score:.4f}")
    Lime deletion score: 0.0317
IntegratedGradients deletion score: 0.0926
Occlusion deletion score: 0.0962

    1.5 Going further: global explanations¶

    For a given sample, we listed the most important words.

    But what are the most important words for a given class?

    We reuse the loaded test subset and request word-level LIME attributions for all occupation classes in a single explain call. This lets Interpreto share the perturbations and model evaluations across targets. Each returned AttributionOutput contains a score matrix of shape (number of classes, number of words). For each class, we count how often a word appears among a biography's three highest-scoring words, then display the ten most frequent words across the test subset.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    from collections import Counter

explainer = Lime(model, tokenizer, n_perturbations=200)

# Compute attributions for the test set on all classes.
all_targets = torch.arange(len(classes_names)).expand(len(test_inputs), -1)
global_attributions = explainer.explain(test_inputs, all_targets)

word_counts = [Counter() for _ in classes_names]
for attribution in global_attributions:
    # Rows follow the class order specified in all_targets.
    top_indices = attribution.attributions.topk(3, dim=-1).indices.tolist()
    for counts, indices in zip(word_counts, top_indices, strict=True):
        # Count a word at most once per biography, ignoring case.
        top_words = {attribution.elements[i].strip().lower() for i in indices}
        counts.update(sorted(top_words - {""}))

for class_name, counts in zip(classes_names, word_counts, strict=True):
    print(f"{class_name}: {[word for word, _ in counts.most_common(5)]}")
    from collections import Counter explainer = Lime(model, tokenizer, n_perturbations=200) # Compute attributions for the test set on all classes. all_targets = torch.arange(len(classes_names)).expand(len(test_inputs), -1) global_attributions = explainer.explain(test_inputs, all_targets) word_counts = [Counter() for _ in classes_names] for attribution in global_attributions: # Rows follow the class order specified in all_targets. top_indices = attribution.attributions.topk(3, dim=-1).indices.tolist() for counts, indices in zip(word_counts, top_indices, strict=True): # Count a word at most once per biography, ignoring case. top_words = {attribution.elements[i].strip().lower() for i in indices} counts.update(sorted(top_words - {""})) for class_name, counts in zip(classes_names, word_counts, strict=True): print(f"{class_name}: {[word for word, _ in counts.most_common(5)]}")

    2. Probing the gender concept¶

    2.1 Split the model and compute activations¶

    We split the model between the encoder $enc$ and the classification head $cls$ thanks to the splitter. Then compute the activations $z$ as the output of the encoder (they correspond to the [CLS] token).

    $f = cls \circ enc$

    $z = enc(x)$

    We use Interpreto's SplitterForClassification and its get_activations() method to extract these representations.

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    from interpreto import SplitterForClassification

# instantiate the splitter from the model
splitter = SplitterForClassification(
    model,
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
    device_map=device,
    batch_size=32,
)

# compute their activations
train_acts, train_occ_preds = splitter.get_activations(train_inputs, tqdm_bar=True, forward_kwargs={"truncation": True})
test_acts, test_occ_preds = splitter.get_activations(test_inputs, tqdm_bar=True, forward_kwargs={"truncation": True})
    from interpreto import SplitterForClassification # instantiate the splitter from the model splitter = SplitterForClassification( model, tokenizer=tokenizer, device_map=device, batch_size=32, ) # compute their activations train_acts, train_occ_preds = splitter.get_activations(train_inputs, tqdm_bar=True, forward_kwargs={"truncation": True}) test_acts, test_occ_preds = splitter.get_activations(test_inputs, tqdm_bar=True, forward_kwargs={"truncation": True})

    2.2 Train a linear probe to predict gender from activations (CAV)¶

    We train a linear SVM as in the original CAV (Concept Activation Vector) paper [1]. Interpreto's LinearSVMProbe learns the gender direction from activations, and ProbeExplainer links it with the splitter.

    $$ s(z) = w^T z + b $$

    [1] Kim et al. - ICML 2018 - Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)

    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    from interpreto.concepts.probes import LinearSVMProbe, ProbeExplainer

# Creating the probe model and linking it with the splitter
probe = LinearSVMProbe(lr=1e-2, max_iter=200, normalization=None)
probe_explainer = ProbeExplainer(splitter, probe)
probe_explainer.to(device)

# Training the probe classifier
probe_explainer.fit(train_acts.to(device), train_genders.float().unsqueeze(1).to(device))
    from interpreto.concepts.probes import LinearSVMProbe, ProbeExplainer # Creating the probe model and linking it with the splitter probe = LinearSVMProbe(lr=1e-2, max_iter=200, normalization=None) probe_explainer = ProbeExplainer(splitter, probe) probe_explainer.to(device) # Training the probe classifier probe_explainer.fit(train_acts.to(device), train_genders.float().unsqueeze(1).to(device))

    We then test the probe's performance to see if the gender concept is linearly accessible from the model's activations.

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    # Validating the probe performance
with torch.no_grad():
    test_scores = probe_explainer.activations_to_concepts(test_acts.to(device))
test_gender_preds = (test_scores.squeeze(1) > 0).long()
accuracy = (test_gender_preds == test_genders.cuda()).float().mean().item()
print(f"test gender probe accuracy: {accuracy:.3f}")
    # Validating the probe performance with torch.no_grad(): test_scores = probe_explainer.activations_to_concepts(test_acts.to(device)) test_gender_preds = (test_scores.squeeze(1) > 0).long() accuracy = (test_gender_preds == test_genders.cuda()).float().mean().item() print(f"test gender probe accuracy: {accuracy:.3f}")
    test gender probe accuracy: 1.000

    2.3 Compute the TCAV score¶

    TCAV for Testing with CAVs check if the concept was used in the prediction. It checks sensibility of the model outputs to the concept direction.

    CAV: $w$

    TCAV: $\nabla_z cls(z) \cdot w$

    This is not directly implemented in interpreto, so we rely on the splitter's _get_concept_output_gradients to obtain the gradients. But it is a work around, future versions will allow simpler solutions for this.

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    import torch.nn.functional as F

class TCAV():
    threshold: None | float = None

    def __init__(self, explainer: ProbeExplainer):
        cav = explainer.concept_model.weight.detach().squeeze()
        self.cav = cav / cav.norm()
        self.splitter = explainer.splitter

    def gradients(self, inputs: list[str] | torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        """
        Compute the gradients using the splitter methods.

        Args:
            inputs:
                (list[str]): The text samples or
                (torch.Tensor): Their activations. (n, d)
        Returns:
            (torch.Tensor): The gradients. (n, cls,d)
        """
        gradients_list = splitter._get_concept_output_gradients(
            inputs=inputs,
            activations_to_concepts=lambda z: z,  # identity: differentiate in activation space
            concepts_to_activations=lambda z: z,  # identity: no concept-space reconstruction
            concepts_x_gradients=False,
        )
        return torch.stack(gradients_list).squeeze().cuda()

    def calibrate(self, gradients: torch.Tensor, percentile: float = 0.95, sampling: int = 100):
        """
        Fixes a threshold to later determine if directions are meaningful.
        The threshold is based on randomly sampled directions.

        Args:
            gradients: The gradients of the outputs with respects to the activations (n, cls, d)
            percentile: CAVs are deamned meaningful if their absolute score is greater than {percentile}.
            sampling: The number of random directions to sample.
        """
        torch.manual_seed(0)
        random_directions = F.normalize(torch.randn(self.cav.shape[0], sampling, device=device), dim=0)  # (d, s)
        t_random = gradients @ random_directions  # (n, cls, s)
        self.threshold = torch.quantile(t_random.abs().permute(1, 0, 2).flatten(1, 2), 0.95, dim=-1)  # (cls,)

    def __call__(self, gradients: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        """
        Args:
            gradients: The gradients of the activations to outputs function with respect to the activations (n, cls, d).
        Returns:
            (torch.Tensor): The TCAV scores. (n, cls)
        """
        return gradients @ self.cav
    import torch.nn.functional as F class TCAV(): threshold: None | float = None def __init__(self, explainer: ProbeExplainer): cav = explainer.concept_model.weight.detach().squeeze() self.cav = cav / cav.norm() self.splitter = explainer.splitter def gradients(self, inputs: list[str] | torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Compute the gradients using the splitter methods. Args: inputs: (list[str]): The text samples or (torch.Tensor): Their activations. (n, d) Returns: (torch.Tensor): The gradients. (n, cls,d) """ gradients_list = splitter._get_concept_output_gradients( inputs=inputs, activations_to_concepts=lambda z: z, # identity: differentiate in activation space concepts_to_activations=lambda z: z, # identity: no concept-space reconstruction concepts_x_gradients=False, ) return torch.stack(gradients_list).squeeze().cuda() def calibrate(self, gradients: torch.Tensor, percentile: float = 0.95, sampling: int = 100): """ Fixes a threshold to later determine if directions are meaningful. The threshold is based on randomly sampled directions. Args: gradients: The gradients of the outputs with respects to the activations (n, cls, d) percentile: CAVs are deamned meaningful if their absolute score is greater than {percentile}. sampling: The number of random directions to sample. """ torch.manual_seed(0) random_directions = F.normalize(torch.randn(self.cav.shape[0], sampling, device=device), dim=0) # (d, s) t_random = gradients @ random_directions # (n, cls, s) self.threshold = torch.quantile(t_random.abs().permute(1, 0, 2).flatten(1, 2), 0.95, dim=-1) # (cls,) def __call__(self, gradients: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Args: gradients: The gradients of the activations to outputs function with respect to the activations (n, cls, d). Returns: (torch.Tensor): The TCAV scores. (n, cls) """ return gradients @ self.cav
    In [15]:
    Copied! 
    # Construct and calibrate TCAV
tcav = TCAV(probe_explainer)
gradients = tcav.gradients(test_inputs)  # We need a certain number for calibration
tcav.calibrate(gradients)

# Compute scores on our studied samples
studied_gradients = tcav.gradients(studied_texts)
for sample, pred, grad in zip(studied_texts, studied_preds, studied_gradients, strict=True):
    score = tcav(grad)[pred]
    feminine_impact = (score > tcav.threshold[pred]).item()
    print(f"Sample: {sample}\nPredicted class: {classes_names[pred]}, TCAV score: {score.item():.4f}, Feminine impact: {feminine_impact}\n")
    # Construct and calibrate TCAV tcav = TCAV(probe_explainer) gradients = tcav.gradients(test_inputs) # We need a certain number for calibration tcav.calibrate(gradients) # Compute scores on our studied samples studied_gradients = tcav.gradients(studied_texts) for sample, pred, grad in zip(studied_texts, studied_preds, studied_gradients, strict=True): score = tcav(grad)[pred] feminine_impact = (score > tcav.threshold[pred]).item() print(f"Sample: {sample}\nPredicted class: {classes_names[pred]}, TCAV score: {score.item():.4f}, Feminine impact: {feminine_impact}\n")

Her philosophy as a designer is to attempt understand the culture, values and intentions at play in each design problem she is faced with, in order to reach a more appropriate and meaningful solution. Griscel currently holds a B.Arch from the Boston Architectural college.
Predicted class: interior_designer, TCAV score: 0.0832, Feminine impact: True

    2.4 Going further: Global classes sensitivity to gender¶

    We were able to measure the gender concept impact on the model's predictions. But we can go further and measure the impact of gender on each class.

    This means computing the gender impact on the model's predictions for each sample and counting the proportions of samples impacted in each class.

    In [16]:
    Copied!

    3. Unsupervised concepts analysis¶

    3.1 Splitting the model and computing activations¶

    Already done in section 2.1.

    3.2 Learn concepts¶

    We use the SemiNMF (a relaxed version of the Non-negative Matrix Factorization) to learn the concepts. It decomposes activations $A = enc(X)$ into a product of concept activations $Z$ and concept vectors $W$:

    $$ A = ZW $$

    We fit SemiNMFConcepts on the training activations to learn 50 concepts.

    In [18]:
    Copied! 
    from interpreto.concepts import SemiNMFConcepts

# instantiate from the splitter
concept_explainer = SemiNMFConcepts(splitter, nb_concepts=50, device=device)

# learn concepts as patterns in the activations
concept_explainer.fit(train_acts.to(device), max_iter=500)
    from interpreto.concepts import SemiNMFConcepts # instantiate from the splitter concept_explainer = SemiNMFConcepts(splitter, nb_concepts=50, device=device) # learn concepts as patterns in the activations concept_explainer.fit(train_acts.to(device), max_iter=500)

    3.3 Interpret concepts¶

    Concepts are currently abstract directions in the activation space; we need to assign them meaning. For each concept, we find the words and short phrases that activate it most strongly.

    $$ topk(cpt) = topk_X\ enc(x) \cdot W_{cpt} $$

    We use TopKInputs to retrieve five examples per concept, considering phrases of up to three words.

    In [19]:
    Copied! 
    from interpreto.concepts.interpretations import TopKInputs

topk = TopKInputs(
    concept_explainer=concept_explainer,
    k=5,
    use_unique_words=3,  # extend up to 3-words ngrams
    unique_words_kwargs={
        "count_min_threshold": max(1, round(len(test_inputs) * 0.002)),  # present in at least 0.2% of the inputs
        "lemmatize": True,
    },
)
interpretations = topk.interpret(inputs=test_inputs)
interpretations = {str(k): list(v.keys()) for k, v in interpretations.items()}
    from interpreto.concepts.interpretations import TopKInputs topk = TopKInputs( concept_explainer=concept_explainer, k=5, use_unique_words=3, # extend up to 3-words ngrams unique_words_kwargs={ "count_min_threshold": max(1, round(len(test_inputs) * 0.002)), # present in at least 0.2% of the inputs "lemmatize": True, }, ) interpretations = topk.interpret(inputs=test_inputs) interpretations = {str(k): list(v.keys()) for k, v in interpretations.items()}

    3.4 Estimate concepts importance¶

    Concepts might be present but not relevant for the predictions. This step evaluates the global importance of concepts with respect to each class.

    The importance is given by the average (over samples) of the concepts to outputs gradients weighted by the concepts activations: $$ mean(\nabla_z cls(ZW) \cdot Z) $$

    We compute these scores with the explainer's concept_output_gradient method and average them over the test samples.

    In [20]:
    Copied! 
    gradients_list = concept_explainer.concept_output_gradient(
    test_acts, targets=None, tqdm_bar=True, normalization=False, concepts_x_gradients=True
)
importances = torch.stack(gradients_list).squeeze().mean(0).cpu()  # (cls, cpt)
    gradients_list = concept_explainer.concept_output_gradient( test_acts, targets=None, tqdm_bar=True, normalization=False, concepts_x_gradients=True ) importances = torch.stack(gradients_list).squeeze().mean(0).cpu() # (cls, cpt)

    You need to click on the classes names to see the relevant concepts.

plot_concepts(classes_names=classes_names, concepts_importances=importances, concepts_labels=interpretations, top_k=5)
